c.text: Chapter 7 – The Conversation You’re Avoiding
You already know who it’s with
Before you read another line, name the person.
There is one – a volunteer who keeps arriving late, someone whose comment last month is still sitting in you, a team member whose attitude everyone has noticed and nobody has addressed.
You know who it is. You have known for weeks. You have rehearsed the conversation in the car and not had it.
This chapter is about why that costs more than you think, and how to actually do it.
Avoidance is not patience
New leaders tell themselves several stories about why they are waiting.
I’m praying about it.
Sometimes true. Often it means waiting for the situation to resolve itself so you never have to speak.
I don’t want to make it worse.
It is already worse. Unaddressed problems do not hold still; they harden into a permanent feature of the team.
“I’m not the right person.” Sometimes you are responsible for the conversation; sometimes it belongs with your manager, a safeguarding lead or another qualified person. Clarify that before acting.
It’s not that serious.
Then why are you still thinking about it in the shower?
One common reason is fear of upsetting someone.
Other reasons include uncertainty, a power imbalance or a genuine risk of retaliation. Work out what is making you hesitate before assuming the answer is simply more courage.
The kindest leaders I know are not the ones who avoid hard conversations. They are the ones who have them early, while they are still small.
Jesus gave a procedure, and he made it personal

Matthew 18:15-17 is the clearest process Jesus gives for handling a wrong between believers. He places it, significantly, immediately after the parable of the shepherd leaving ninety-nine sheep to go after one that wandered – the whole framing is recovery, not punishment.

The steps: go and point out the fault just between the two of you. If they listen, you have won them over. If not, take one or two others along, so that every matter may be established by two or three witnesses. If they still refuse to listen, tell it to the church.

Three details matter enormously and are routinely ignored. For an ordinary interpersonal wrong, the passage begins with a private approach. That does not forbid confidential advice or require a person to confront someone who may harm them. Safeguarding concerns, abuse and suspected crime require the appropriate reporting process, not a compulsory private meeting.
It starts with you going. Jesus does not say wait for them to come to you.
The stated goal is winning the person, not winning the argument. If your aim in the conversation is to be proved right, you are not doing what this passage describes.

And then look at Matthew 5:23-24, from the Sermon on the Mount. Jesus says that if you are offering your gift at the altar and remember that your brother has something against you, leave the gift, go and be reconciled, and then come and offer it.
Read that carefully.
In this passage they have something against you. And you are still the one who goes.
Between the two passages, whichever direction the offence runs, the instruction to you is the same: go.
Before you go: two proverbs that will save you
Proverbs 18:13 says that answering before listening is folly and shame. Proverbs 18:17 adds that the first to present his case seems right, until another comes forward and questions him.
You are walking in with one side of the story. Possibly your own. There is a decent chance that what you are certain about is partly wrong.

The volunteer who keeps arriving late may be caring for a parent every morning and be too proud to say so. The comment that offended you may have been about something entirely different. The team member with the bad attitude may have been promised something by a previous leader that nobody told you about.
So go in to find out, not to deliver a verdict. This changes the whole shape of the conversation and it is why the opening sentence matters so much.
How to actually do it
Choose an appropriate setting and format.

A private, unhurried conversation is often best, but a phone call, video call or carefully written exchange may be more accessible or safer. Avoid a rushed confrontation before a service. Follow safeguarding arrangements and allow an appropriate support person where needed.
Open with observation, not accusation.
There is a simple structure that works:
What I’ve noticed… what I assumed… and I want to check whether I’ve got that right.

For example: “I’ve noticed you’ve arrived after we start for the last three weeks. I assumed something might have changed at home, but I don’t actually know. What’s going on?” Compare that to “You’ve been late three weeks running.” Same fact, completely different conversation.
Then stop talking.
Ask the question and let the silence sit. Most new leaders fill it and lose everything the person was about to say.
Address the behaviour, not the character.
“The set-up wasn’t done twice this month” is workable. “You’re unreliable” is a label, and people defend labels rather than fix behaviour.
Say what you need, specifically.
End with a clear, concrete request and a check that they have agreed to it. “Can you be here by 9:15, or should we move you to the later service where the timing works better?”
Leave a door open.
Offer a change of role, a break, or help, where that is honest. You are trying to keep this person.
Speaking the truth in love is one act, not two

Ephesians 4:15 tells the church to speak the truth in love, so that we grow up into Christ. Paul is describing how a body matures – the honesty and the love are not in tension, they are the same movement.
Most of us collapse it in one of two directions.
We are loving and never truthful, so nothing changes and resentment builds. Or we are truthful and not loving, and we win the point and lose the person.
Galatians 6:1 gives the posture.
Paul says that if someone is caught in a sin, those who are spiritual should restore that person gently – and then he adds: watch yourself, or you also may be tempted.
Restore.

Gently. Watch yourself. The last one is the safeguard against the quiet self-righteousness that hard conversations can breed in leaders. You are going to correct someone in an area where you are not perfect either, and remembering that will keep your voice right.

Proverbs 15:1 reminds us that a gentle answer can de-escalate conflict, while harsh words can inflame it. Your tone matters, but it does not control the other person’s behaviour or make you responsible for their aggression.
If it goes badly
If they get angry, remain calm and offer a pause.
You can say, “Would you like to continue, or should we agree another time?” End the conversation if there are threats, intimidation or a safety concern, and seek appropriate support.
If they cry, stop pressing.
Ask if there is something else going on. Very often there is.

If they disagree with your account, listen and check the facts. Distinguish what you observed from what you inferred. Agree any clear expectations and a review date, and use a fair process for disputed allegations rather than trying to force a confession. If an ordinary disagreement does not resolve, seek suitable help through the church’s agreed process. Explain why others are involved and give the person an opportunity to respond. Serious misconduct and safeguarding concerns need their own procedures.

If it’s about you – if they raise something you did – resist explaining. Say “let me think about that properly” and mean it. A leader who can receive correction without defending will be trusted with almost anything.
And when it still doesn’t work out
Romans 12:18 is realistic in a way that ought to relieve you: if it is possible, as far as it depends on you, live at peace with everyone.
Two qualifiers in one short verse.
Paul, writing to a mixed and strained church in Rome, knows that some peace is not achievable, and that the other person’s part is not yours to control.
Remember also Paul and Barnabas in Acts 15:39, whose disagreement over John Mark was sharp enough that they separated and went in different directions – and God kept working through both of them.
Do your part promptly, gently and through the appropriate route. Then recognise what is beyond your control.
